c: [TOC] ## Solution --- ### Approach 1: Brute Force #### Intuition Let's try to learn which letters end up bold, since the resulting answer will just be the canonical one - we put bold tags around each group of bold letters. To do this, we'll check for all occurrences of each word and mark the corresponding letters bold. #### Algorithm Let's work on first setting `mask[i] = true` if and only if the `i`-th letter is bold. For each starting position `i` in `S`, for each word, if `S[i]` starts with word, we'll set the appropriate letters bold. Now armed with the correct mask, let's try to output the answer. A letter in position `i` is the first bold letter of the group if `mask[i] && (i == 0 || !mask[i-1])`, and is the last bold letter if `mask[i] && (i == N-1 || !mask[i+1])`. Alternatively, we could use `itertools.groupby` in Python. Once we know which letters are the first and last bold letters of a group, we know where to put the `""` and `""` tags. #### Implementation #### Complexity Analysis Let $N$ be the length of $S$ and $\sum w_i$ be the total length of all words. - Time complexity: $O(N \sum w_i)$ For each of the $N$ starting positions in $S$, we check every word to see if it matches. Each check takes $O(w_i)$ time per word, so the total time is $O(N \sum w_i)$. - Space complexity: $O(N)$ The mask array stores a boolean for each character in $S$. --- ### Approach 2: Aho-Corasick #### Intuition The brute force approach checks every word at every position separately. With the Aho-Corasick algorithm, we preprocess all words into a single finite automaton (a trie extended with failure links) so that one left-to-right scan of $S$ finds all occurrences of all words simultaneously. **Trie and failure links:** We first insert all words into a trie. Each node represents a matched prefix of one or more words. As we scan $S$ character by character, we follow edges in the trie. When a node has no edge for the current character, we cannot extend the current match — but instead of restarting from scratch, a failure link sends us to the longest proper suffix of the currently matched prefix that is also a prefix in the trie. This is the same idea as the KMP algorithm, extended to multiple patterns. For example, if the words are `["he", "she", "his", "hers"]` and we have matched `"she"`, the failure link from the `"she"` node points to `"he"`, so matching `"he"` costs no extra work. **Goto optimization:** During BFS construction of failure links, whenever node $u$ has no child for character $c$, we set `nxt[u][c] = nxt[fail[u]][c]`. This precomputes the destination after a mismatch, so every character transition in $S$ is $O(1)$ with no chasing of failure links at query time. **Propagating word lengths:** When we reach state $u$ after processing $S[i]$, any word that ends at $u$ directly or at any node reachable via the chain of failure links from $u$ matches as a suffix of $S[0..i]$. By propagating the maximum word length through failure links during BFS — `maxWordLen[u] = max(maxWordLen[u], maxWordLen[fail[u]])` — each node stores the length of the longest such word. A single lookup at query time is enough. **Marking bold positions:** Knowing that a word of length $L$ ends at position $i$ tells us the range $[i - L + 1,\ i]$ should be bold. Instead of marking every position in that range immediately (which could be $O(N \cdot W_{\max})$ overall), we record only the right endpoint in a `right` array indexed by the start of the match. A single left-to-right sweep with a running maximum `reach` then determines all bold positions in $O(N)$. #### Algorithm 1. Build a trie from all words. At each terminal node, record the length of the word that ends there. 2. Construct failure links via BFS. For each node $u$ processed in BFS order: - Set `maxWordLen[u] = max(maxWordLen[u], maxWordLen[fail[u]])` to propagate the longest matching word length through suffix links. - For each character $c$: if $u$ has a child $v$ for $c$, set `fail[v] = nxt[fail[u]][c]` and enqueue $v$. Otherwise apply the goto optimization: set `nxt[u][c] = nxt[fail[u]][c]`. 3. Traverse $S$ through the automaton. After processing each character $S[i]$, if `maxWordLen[cur] > 0`, a word of that length ends at position $i$ and starts at $\text{start} = i - \text{maxWordLen}[\text{cur}] + 1$. Update `right[start] = max(right[start], i)`. 4. Sweep `right` left to right with a running maximum `reach`. Position $i$ is bold if `reach >= i`. 5. Build the output string, inserting `` and `` at the boundaries of bold groups. #### Implementation #### Complexity Analysis Let $N$ be the length of $S$ and $M = \sum w_i$ be the total length of all words. - Time complexity: $O(M \cdot \Sigma + N)$ Building the trie takes $O(M)$ time. Constructing failure links via BFS takes $O(M \cdot \Sigma)$ since each of the at most $M$ nodes processes all $\Sigma = 26$ characters. Traversing $S$ takes $O(N)$ because each transition is $O(1)$ after the goto optimization. The bold-marking sweep is also $O(N)$. - Space complexity: $O(M \cdot \Sigma + N)$ The automaton stores at most $M$ nodes each with $\Sigma$ transitions, using $O(M \cdot \Sigma)$ space. The auxiliary arrays (`right`, `bold`) use $O(N)$ space. ---
